classification.reasoning: Purpose: The crate is named 'serde-jsonn', which is a clear typosquatting attempt targeting the immensely popular 'serde_json' crate (edit distance 1, matching pattern-typosquatting). Sources: Its build script reads a sensitive environment variable, 'SECRET_KEY'. Sinks: The build script attempts a network connection via `TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:8890")`. Flow: The build script reads the sensitive secret from the environment and passes it out via a network socket during compilation (`cargo build`), before any normal application code runs. Anomalies: The package contains almost no meaningful source code (8 lines of total Rust code), zero dependencies, and executes dangerous build-script actions that match classic supply-chain credential-harvesting attacks. Conclusion: The combination of high-confidence typosquatting and environment variable exfiltration via a build script confirms intentional maliciousness.

retrieved_context.title: General pattern: legitimate build.rs signals that are NOT malicious
retrieved_context.text: Common benign reasons a crate's build.rs may trigger a raw signal match: checking the installed rustc/cargo version via Command::new (used by serde and many other major crates to gate feature availability); generating code from a schema or protobuf definition, sometimes fetched over network from a first-party, well-known source; reading a small number of standard, non-sensitive environment variables like OUT_DIR, TARGET, or CARGO_PKG_VERSION which Cargo itself sets. A high-quality classifier should not flag these alone -- context (destination of network calls, sensitivity of specific env var names read, and the crate's stated purpose) matters more than raw signal presence.
retrieved_context.source: synthesized from observed benign build.rs behavior, e.g. serde

retrieved_context.title: General pattern: typosquatting / impersonation
retrieved_context.text: Attackers register crate names with small edit distances from popular, widely-trusted crates, relying on developer typos or visual similarity (underscore vs hyphen, 0 vs o, added/removed pluralization) to get pulled as an accidental dependency. A typosquat alone is not proof of malicious intent (some near-duplicate names are legitimate forks or abandoned-name reuse), but a typosquat COMBINED with any build.rs network/env signal, or with a very new/low-reputation publishing account, sharply raises confidence.

retrieved_context.title: CrateDepression / rustdecimal (2022)
retrieved_context.text: A coordinated typosquatting campaign where the crate 'rustdecimal' impersonated the legitimate 'rust_decimal' crate (52M+ downloads at the time). Edit distance from the target name was 1 (removed underscore). The malicious crate's build.rs deployed a Mythic C2 (command and control) agent specifically into GitLab CI/CD pipelines. The payload fingerprinted the environment before activating -- it only deployed inside detected CI systems, evading casual local testing. Attack category: typosquatting + backdoor + CI-targeting build.rs payload.
